one_line: Proof-of-condition at the dock door: cameras plus a small vision model that count pallets and cartons, capture damage photos, read labels and BOLs, and reconcile against the WMS before the driver leaves.

problem.summary: Receiving is still counted by hand and documented with a clipboard or a phone camera roll. When a shortage or damage surfaces days later, the freight claim clock is already running and the only evidence is a clean signature on the delivery receipt. Federal rules require a written claim with shipment-identifying facts and a stated amount within at least nine months, and explicitly say that notations on a delivery receipt or a bad-order report do not by themselves constitute a claim. Small 3PLs and distributors therefore absorb chargebacks they could have disproven, or they pay staff to reconstruct what happened from video that has already looped over.

evidence.fact: Middlesex County has 1,305 transportation and warehousing establishments employing 49,911 people in 2024 - 13.3% of county private employment versus 6.4% statewide - and the sector grew 26.1% from 2018 to 2024, the fastest of any sector in the county.

Shipping, receiving and inventory clerks in the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro (which contains Middlesex County) averaged $23.08/hour and $48,000/year across 40,440 jobs; hand freight/stock laborers averaged $20.66/hour and $42,970/year across 130,180 jobs.
A carrier may not set a claim filing window shorter than 9 months, or a lawsuit window shorter than 2 years after a written denial (Carmack Amendment, 49 U.S.C. 14706).
Carriers must pay, decline or make a firm written settlement offer within 120 days of receiving a cargo claim, and re-advise the claimant every 60 days while it stays pending (49 CFR 370.9).

Notations of shortage or damage on a freight bill or delivery receipt, and carrier bad-order or inspection reports, 'standing alone' do not meet the minimum federal claim filing requirements - a written claim with a specified or determinable amount is required (49 CFR 370.3(b)-(c)).

A survey of more than 300 shippers, carriers and 3PLs found most believe they are not at fault for up to 70-90% of the OS&D claims they pay; the survey was run by Kargo with FreightWaves, so treat the figure as vendor-sponsored.

A peer-reviewed warehouse performance study models receiving error rates of 1%-10% across warehouse types, with 3.5% as its 'typical' scenario input. These are model inputs, not a measured field rate.
evidence.year: 2019-2021 (article; exact year not confirmed on the abstract page)

evidence.fact: Vendor research puts the LTL industry damage rate at about 1.24% of shipments (roughly 1 in 80), and reports a 0.81% rate across 851,978 shipments for a two-touch cross-dock model versus the five-touch terminal model. Company research, not an independent audit.

A 2018 survey of retail vendors (Attain Consulting Group with the Credit Research Foundation) found median non-trade deductions at 0.5-1% of accounts receivable for vendors under $500M revenue, and 48% of vendors set no time limit before writing a chargeback off entirely.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 10-200 staff, 2-20 dock doors; pain starts at the second client and the second door
buyers.why: Every OS&D dispute is billed back to a client relationship, not just to insurance; the 3PL is presumed liable at origin without condition evidence. Multi-client sites also need per-client photo/claim packages, which is exactly what manual phone photos fail to produce consistently.

buyers.business_type: Wholesale distributors (grocery, building materials, auto parts, industrial supply)
buyers.why: They both receive from vendors and ship to retail DCs. Retail compliance programs fine on-time/in-full and labeling/pallet defects, so a receiving count that does not reconcile to the PO shows up later as a chargeback or a short-ship to the retailer.

buyers.business_type: E-commerce fulfillment / DTC brands running their own ship-from-stock
buyers.why: Small-parcel carrier claims and customer damage complaints are decided on photos and timestamps; a dock-level photo record per outbound pallet/tote is the cheapest evidence to produce.

buyers.business_type: Freight forwarders, cross-dock and container devanning operations
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-75 staff, 2-12 doors or a devanning bay
buyers.why: Container devanning and cross-docking have the shortest dwell time and the worst evidence trail; damage is discovered after the container is empty and the driver is gone.

buyers.business_type: Food and beverage distributors with cold/dry receiving
buyers.why: Damage and temperature exposure on inbound pallets is a rejection decision made at the door; a photo record plus time stamp supports both rejection and the vendor chargeback.

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cameras at each outbound dock door read SKUs, LPNs and lot codes as pallets load, flag damaged cases/broken pallets/unexpected SKUs, and validate against WMS order data (flat-file/SFTP or API integration).

Fixed unit at a wrap station that counts and verifies pallets, captures images and dimensions, keeps raw video on-site and sends only results and metadata to the cloud. Aimed at pallet manufacturing/repair operations as much as shipping docks.
existing_solutions.pricing: $1,995 hardware per unit with 1-year warranty + $595/month per unit software (unlimited users)

existing_solutions.product: Dock camera shipment inspection / claims management
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Uses dock cameras plus WMS/TMS data to build visual evidence for freight and OS&D claims and to detect fraudulent or mis-timed claims.

Phone or fixed-bay photos/video of an inbound consignment are turned into carton counts, PO line matching, crush/puncture/moisture checks and a WMS exception ticket; arithmetic reconciliation is done in code rather than by the model.
existing_solutions.pricing: EUR 0.05 per verified consignment, pay-as-you-go, no seat fees

existing_solutions.product: Custom warehouse pallet counting on existing cameras
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Connects to existing RTSP/ONVIF dock cameras, counts pallets per door with direction tracking, reconciles camera counts to WMS scans, sends a photo alert when a pallet leaves unscanned, runs an on-site analysis server. Sold as a fixed-price project, 6-10 weeks.
existing_solutions.pricing: From $8,000 per project (fixed estimate after site survey)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Dock-door concept device mounted on the door track guards that counts and photographs every pallet, calls open edges/trailer creep and slows forklifts. The vendor labels it a 'VisionConcept', so the price is a target, not a shipping product.

Phone/tablet receiving inspections with photos, counts, signatures, AI damage flagging for the receiver to confirm, offline capture, and a PDF claims packet per inspection; damage rates by carrier, vendor and site.
existing_solutions.pricing: Per-site subscription, unlimited users; the exact price was not shown on the page I opened - Unknown

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Dock-door pallet identification and load verification with a free two-day proof of value on one gate, aimed at missed pallets and wrong loadings.

gap_for_local_installer: The market splits into two unattractive halves for a 5-200 person Middlesex County operator. Enterprise dock-vision (Kargo, Arvist, Zimark) is quote-only, multi-week, and priced per door per month for national fleets; app-only tools (CargoLens, generic inspection apps) still depend on a human remembering to photograph and count, which is the failure mode in the first place. Published prices cluster around $1,290-$1,995 of hardware per door plus $595/month, or a ~$8,000 fixed project - small enough to sell, but the products are either single-purpose (pallet counting only) or oriented to pallet manufacturing, not to a 3PL's inbound PO/ASN reconciliation. Nobody local is doing camera + model + WMS wiring as a fixed-price, on-prem install with a service contract. The wedge is: reuse the customer's existing RTSP dock cameras where possible, one on-prem box per site (no per-door cloud fee, no raw video leaving the building), integrate to whatever the customer actually runs (Extensiv 3PL Warehouse Manager REST API, ShipHero GraphQL, Fishbowl, or a nightly CSV), and produce two artifacts the incumbent tools under-serve: a per-receipt exception ticket with a photo bundle, and a per-pallet evidence packet that matches federal claim requirements. Local presence is the moat: same-day site visits, install in a weekend, and a human who answers when the count disputes a client.

technical_approach.established_pattern: Fixed PoE camera per dock door (overhead or 30-45 degrees off the door line), RTSP into an on-prem edge box. A fine-tuned YOLO-family detector finds pallets and carton faces per frame; a tracker assigns IDs and gives direction so the system counts a pallet once as it crosses the door line (zone rule per door) rather than per frame. On each crossing the box grabs a few high-resolution frames, runs a small vision-language model to read the pallet label / BOL / PO number and to write a short damage description, then reconciles the extracted text and count against the WMS expected shipment in ordinary code (regex plus arithmetic), never trusting the model to do math. Exceptions become a ticket plus an evidence bundle (frames, timestamps, JSON) posted to the WMS; clean receipts auto-commit. Frigate is a reasonable off-the-shelf front end for stream handling, recording and detector plumbing if you do not build your own.

models_and_tools.name: YOLO11 / YOLOv12 (Ultralytics)
models_and_tools.role: Pallet and carton detection backbone; fine-tune on the site's own cartons and wrap. Note the AGPL-3.0 license: closed-source commercial deployment needs a quoted Enterprise License.

models_and_tools.name: SCD - Stacked Carton Dataset
models_and_tools.role: Large-scale public carton detection/segmentation dataset (10k+ annotated stacking scenes) to pretrain or sanity-check a carton detector before site fine-tuning.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL (2B / 4B dense variants)
models_and_tools.role: Reading labels, BOLs and packing slips at the door, and generating a short damage description. The technical report lists dense 2B/4B/8B/32B and MoE variants; the small dense models are the ones that fit an edge box.

models_and_tools.name: LFM2.5-VL-450M (Liquid AI)
models_and_tools.role: Ultra-small VLM alternative for on-device label/damage checks. Vendor benchmarks: 242 ms at 512x512 on Jetson Orin at Q4_0, OCRBench 684, CountBench 73.31 - the low count score is a reason to count with a detector, not the VLM.

models_and_tools.name: llama.cpp
models_and_tools.role: Local serving of the quantized VLM on the edge box, no cloud dependency and no per-image API cost.

models_and_tools.name: PaddleOCR
models_and_tools.role: Cheap deterministic OCR baseline for printed labels and BOL fields; run it before the VLM and only escalate crops it fails on, which cuts compute and hallucination.

models_and_tools.name: PatchCore (anomaly detection)
models_and_tools.role: Damage detection trained only on undamaged carton images - no need to collect examples of every damage type. CVPR 2022 report of 99.1% image-level AUROC on MVTec AD is a lab benchmark, not a dock result.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate
models_and_tools.role: Open-source NVR: RTSP/ONVIF stream handling, motion-triggered detection on a low-res stream plus high-res recording, hardware detectors (Coral Edge TPU, OpenVINO, TensorRT, Hailo, Rockchip, MemryX, AMD ROCm/ONNX), and LPR for yard/door cameras.

models_and_tools.name: Cactus
models_and_tools.role: Open-source on-device inference framework for phones (sub-50MB class agents, vision/audio) if the capture step should run on the receiver's phone instead of a fixed camera.

models_and_tools.name: Extensiv 3PL Warehouse Manager API
models_and_tools.role: The realistic WMS target for small-to-mid NJ 3PLs: REST order endpoints (POST/GET /orders) with RQL filters and bearer-token auth, so expected quantities can be pulled and exception notes written back.

models_and_tools.name: ShipHero GraphQL API
models_and_tools.role: Alternative WMS target for e-commerce fulfillment: inventory_add, purchase_order_update (increment quantity_received) and purchase_order_close cover the receiving write-back path.

hardware.item: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (edge compute per site, 1-3 doors)
Google Coral USB Accelerator (detector offload if not using Jetson GPU)
hardware.approx_cost: About $60 vendor-listed; resellers quoted higher (about $111 at Seeed). Confirm before quoting.

hardware.item: 4MP PoE turret/bullet camera, one per dock door (Hikvision class)
hardware.approx_cost: $105-$168 per camera at a US reseller
$0 if already installed and the angle clears the forklift; Happ Labs reports many sites can reuse existing cameras

hardware.item: Managed PoE switch, cabling, mount arms, small UPS
hardware.approx_cost: Unknown from a primary source; budget as an allowance (inference: a few hundred dollars per door at typical 2026 US trade prices)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Partly. A detector fine-tuned on the site's own cartons, pallet wrap and lighting is normally required - generic COCO models do not separate 'same SKU carton stack' reliably, and the published packaging-recognition work needed its own custom logistics dataset to reach 85-91% structure accuracy. The VLM side usually needs no fine-tuning: prompt the small VLM with a fixed schema ('extract PO number, pallet count, carrier, damage keywords') and validate the output with regex and a PO lookup, escalating failures to a human. Damage detection is best treated as anomaly detection trained on good cartons only, which needs no labelled damage examples. Ongoing drift (new packaging, new wrap) means a re-label and re-train loop every few months - that recurring work is the service contract.
technical_approach.data_needed: Per door: roughly 300-2,000 labelled frames covering that site's carton families, pallet patterns, wrap and lighting (a few hours of video, labelled by drawing boxes, ideally with a week of active learning). Per label type: 50-100 photographed labels/BOLs with ground-truth fields to measure exact-match extraction. Per site: 2-4 weeks of WMS PO/ASN and receipt records so reconciliation can be validated against what actually happened, plus the customer's damage/claim definitions (what counts as 'damaged' is a business rule, not a vision rule). Also needed: a written retention and access policy signed by the customer before go-live.

measured_outcomes.finding: Tillamook (dairy co-op, 7 outbound doors): damage claims down 50% year-over-year, $173,000 in fees and chargebacks avoided in 2025, 42 customer claims refuted with photo/sensor evidence, inventory accuracy 99.6% to 99.8%, vendor-reported read rate >99% and OCR accuracy >99%, 31-second event-to-alert latency.
Neovia Logistics (UK) reported claims reduced by 40% and faster evidence-based claim decisions after deploying Octave Coda video insight at its sites.
measured_outcomes.sample: One 3PL customer; site count not stated in the excerpt

measured_outcomes.finding: YOLOv12 damaged-parcel detector trained on 5,188 labelled images reached 93.3% precision, 93.8% recall and 93.7% mAP@0.50 on a 7% held-out test split.
measured_outcomes.sample: 5,188 images, 7% test split; single dataset, no field deployment

measured_outcomes.finding: Automated packaging-structure recognition from a single image (count and arrangement of packaging units on a transport unit) correctly recognized the structure in about 85% of test cases, rising to 91% when restricted to the most common package types.
measured_outcomes.sample: Custom realistic logistics image dataset; size not confirmed from the abstract

measured_outcomes.finding: PatchCore anomaly detection reached 99.1% image-level AUROC on the MVTec AD industrial defect benchmark using only normal (undamaged) training images.
measured_outcomes.sample: MVTec AD benchmark (15 categories); lab data, not dock cartons

measured_outcomes.finding: Multi-view geometric counting of stacked objects (ICCV 2025 oral) reports accurate counting of identical objects in containers even when irregularly stacked, validated on real-world and large-scale synthetic datasets.
measured_outcomes.sample: Multiple real and synthetic datasets; exact error rates not stated in the abstract

measured_outcomes.finding: Most respondents to a 300+ person shipper/carrier/3PL survey believe they are not at fault for up to 70-90% of the OS&D claims they pay - i.e. the dispute is an evidence problem, not a damage problem.

Median non-trade (logistics) retail deductions equal 0.5-1% of accounts receivable for vendors under $500M revenue, and 48% of vendors never time-limit how long a chargeback stays open before write-off.
measured_outcomes.sample: Retail vendor survey (Attain Consulting Group / Credit Research Foundation); respondent count not stated on the summary page

legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act is one-party consent, N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d); intercepting an oral communication without consent of a party is a third-degree crime under 2A:156A-3, with civil liability under 2A:156A-24. A camera picking up a conversation the operator is not part of is the risk. Design decision: disable audio in the hardware profile and document it.

legal_privacy.issue: Notice to employees for silent video
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey has no statute or regulation specifically governing an employer's use of video recording devices in the workplace; silent video falls outside the wiretap act, but employees retain a common-law right against offensive intrusion, so handbook notice and staying out of break rooms/restrooms is the practical control. This is from a law-firm summary, not from a statute I read directly.

legal_privacy.issue: Direction of NJ notice law (adjacent, not directly applicable)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: P.L. 2021, c.449 (N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22, effective April 18, 2022) requires an employer to give written notice before knowingly using a tracking device in a vehicle an employee uses, with penalties up to $1,000 first violation and $2,500 for each subsequent one. It covers vehicle tracking, not fixed dock cameras, but it is the clearest sign that NJ expects written notice before monitoring.

legal_privacy.issue: NJ Data Privacy Act and worker video
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: The NJDPA (P.L. 2023, c.266) took effect January 15, 2025, but defines 'consumer' as a resident acting only in an individual or household context and expressly excludes a person acting in a commercial or employment context. Warehouse worker footage is therefore largely outside the NJDPA, and the Act's thresholds (100,000 consumers, or 25,000 plus data sale revenue) are far above a small 3PL anyway. Customer/shipper personal data pulled in through BOLs could still be in scope.

New Jersey has no standalone biometric privacy statute; bills to restrict business use of biometric surveillance (e.g. S3182, 2024-2025 session) were introduced but I could not confirm enactment. The FTC's May 18, 2023 Policy Statement on Biometric Information and Section 5 warns that unexpected collection, inadequate vendor oversight, and unsupported accuracy claims can be unfair or deceptive practices. Practical rule for this avenue: do not do face recognition or person identification at all; count objects, not people.

NLRB General Counsel Memorandum GC 23-02 (October 31, 2022) states the GC will argue that always-on electronic surveillance and algorithmic management of employees is presumptively unlawful absent a narrowly tailored business need, and will seek employee disclosure. For a unionized site, adding cameras that can produce discipline is a mandatory subject of bargaining. A receiving-accuracy system that produces footage of named workers should be scoped, noticed and, where a union exists, bargained before install.

Under 49 U.S.C. 14706 and 49 CFR 370.3, a claim must be in writing, identify the shipment, assert liability and state a specified or determinable amount; damage notations on a delivery receipt or a carrier bad-order report do not, standing alone, satisfy the filing requirement. This is the design requirement for the evidence bundle: photo + count + timestamp + written claim value, not just a photo library. 49 CFR 370.9 sets the 120-day carrier response clock.

legal_privacy.issue: False accusation / wrongful discipline from model errors
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No New Jersey statute or reported case I could find addresses AI-generated dock evidence in a discipline or claim dispute. The practical exposure is contractual and reputational: a miscount that blames a named employee or accuses a carrier of a shortage that never happened. Controls: human confirmation before any exception is attributed to a person, 'unknown' as a first-class model output, per-door accuracy reporting, and no automated discipline triggers.

I could not confirm any New Jersey or federal rule setting a retention period for private warehouse video. Retention is a contract and insurance question: long enough to support the federal claim window (claim filing at least 9 months, carrier response 120 days), short enough to limit exposure (inference).

public: Google/Yelp reviews that mention short shipments, crushed cartons, or 'they said it was damaged in transit' - a direct proxy for OS&D disputes reaching customers.

Job postings for receiving clerk, inventory control, OS&D clerk, claims analyst, deduction analyst or 'vendor compliance' - a dedicated chargeback/deduction role means the volume is already large enough to staff.
Number of dock doors and square footage from LoopNet/Crexi listings and satellite view of the building - 2+ doors with a paved yard is the minimum viable install.
Middlesex County scale check: 1,305 transportation and warehousing establishments and 49,911 employees in 2024, the county's fastest-growing sector (NJ LWD QCEW report).

Whether the company's site names a WMS or EDI provider (Extensiv/3PL Central, ShipHero, Fishbowl, Descartes, SPS Commerce) - determines integration difficulty and is often on the careers or integrations page.

Private fleet or carrier relationships via FMCSA SAFER/SMS lookups, and OSHA establishment inspection history via OSHA's establishment search (I attempted osha.gov and received HTTP 403, so this signal is unverified for now).

Customer base type: if they ship to Walmart/Target/Amazon, the retail compliance penalty structure (on-time/in-full, label and pallet defects) means receiving reconciliation errors convert directly into fines.
Whether they advertise 'same-day shipping' or tight cut-off times - speed pressure is where manual counts get skipped.
walk_in: Count the dock doors and look up: is there already a camera over each door, and does its angle see the pallet face or just the trailer?
Watch one receiving event end to end: is someone counting cartons by hand, with a scan gun, or not at all before the driver leaves?
Look for the damage documentation habit - clipboard binder, Sharpie notes on the BOL, or a phone camera roll with no structure. Ask to see what a claim packet looks like today.
Ask where PO/ASN reconciliation happens: WMS module, Excel, or a person's head.
Ask 'how many chargebacks or deductions did you eat last quarter, and who chases them?' and 'what did the last carrier damage claim cost you in staff time?'
Check infrastructure at the doors: PoE switch capacity, cabling, Wi-Fi dead spots, and whether IT is in-house or an MSP (determines install timeline and who signs off).
Note whether workers are unionized and whether there is an existing camera/monitoring policy in the handbook.
Check the yard and staging: is there space for a fixed camera mount and an on-prem box that will not be forklift-bumped?

pilot.scope: One facility, two dock doors, inbound receiving only. Camera captures each pallet crossing; system counts cartons/pallets, photographs damage, OCRs the pallet label and BOL, reconciles to the WMS PO/ASN, and auto-generates an exception ticket plus an evidence packet. One WMS integration (Extensiv 3PL Warehouse Manager REST, ShipHero GraphQL, or a scheduled CSV if there is no API). Human confirms every exception before anything is attributed to a person or a carrier. Runs 4 weeks of install + 2 weeks of parallel running against the manual process.
pilot.hardware: 2 x 4MP PoE cameras (or reuse existing RTSP cameras), 1 x NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super ($399) or a small x86 edge box on premises, PoE switch + mounts + UPS, optional Coral USB for detector offload. On-prem only: raw video stays in the building, only exception frames and metadata sync out.
pilot.success_metric: Primary: count agreement with a manual control count of at least 99% of pallets and within +/-1 carton per pallet on a 100-pallet control sample. Secondary: at least 90% of damage events a supervisor independently agrees are real, each with a usable photo and timestamp; label/PO-number exact-match extraction at least 95%; time from driver arrival to a finished claim evidence packet under 5 minutes (versus a manual reconstruction that typically happens days later - inference); zero pallets leaving with no record.
pilot.cost_range: $6,000-$15,000 for the pilot build (2 doors, hardware, install, model tuning, one WMS integration, 30 days of support), then $300-$800/month per site for monitoring, retraining and support. The range is anchored on published competitor prices: Happ Labs projects from $8,000, PalletVision at $1,995 hardware + $595/month per unit, IEMI DockOne concept at $1,290/door, Sensifai at EUR 0.05 per verification.
pilot.assumptions: Existing network and power at the doors; cameras can be reused or added cheaply (~$105-168 each); the customer can export or expose PO/ASN data; one facility and one WMS; the customer supplies 2-4 weeks of historical receipts for validation and a supervisor for 2-3 hours of labelling review; damage definitions are agreed in writing before go-live; audio recording stays disabled; no face recognition; pricing excludes the customer's own staff time and any WMS vendor integration fees.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is real and quantifiable: federal claim rules put the burden of proof on whoever holds the freight, Middlesex County has 1,305 transportation/warehousing establishments growing 26% since 2018, and vendor surveys suggest most paid OS&D claims are disputed on evidence rather than on facts. Local buyers are dense but the specific 493110 subset is unverified, and a 5-200 staff 3PL's willingness to pay is capped by a labor cost of roughly $23/hour for the clerk being augmented - which is why published competitor prices sit at $1,290-$8,000 rather than $50,000. Technical feasibility is good: off-the-shelf detectors, small VLMs that run in ~240ms on a $399 Jetson, and documented WMS APIs mean no research breakthrough is needed; the hard part is site-specific data and integration, which is exactly the service. Legal risk is moderate-low if audio stays off, faces are not identified, and no automated discipline is offered - but unionized sites and worker-monitoring exposure are real friction. Defensibility is the weakest score: Kargo, Arvist, Zimark and Sensifai already sell this, and a competent integrator could copy the build, so the moat is local service, on-prem data handling, and the claims-packet workflow rather than the model itself.

risks: Incumbent dock-vision vendors (Kargo, Arvist, Zimark, PalletVision) are already selling to this buyer type and can drop price or add a channel program.
Accuracy liability: a missed damaged pallet or a false 'short' accusation damages the customer's carrier and client relationships; a human-in-the-loop step is mandatory and slows the sales pitch.
Small VLMs are weak at counting (LFM2.5-VL-450M scores 73.31 on CountBench), so any design that lets the language model produce counts will fail in the field.
Ultralytics YOLO is AGPL-3.0; closed-source commercial deployment requires a quoted enterprise license, an unplanned cost that must be priced in or avoided with a different detector.
WMS integration is the schedule risk: small 3PLs often run a TMS plus spreadsheets, or a WMS with restricted API access, and the write-back path is where projects slip.
Worker-monitoring blowback: NLRB GC 23-02 signals hostility to always-on surveillance, and unionized warehouses must bargain before install.
Low price ceiling: the labor being replaced costs about $23/hour and per-door competitor pricing is already $595/month, which caps what a small operator will sign.
Damage is subjective; without a written definition agreed up front, every disputed exception becomes an argument about the model rather than about the carton.
Hardware/edge support burden: cameras get bumped by forklifts, lenses get dusty, and PoE runs fail - a service contract must be priced to absorb truck rolls.
caveats: Vendor outcome numbers (Kargo/Tillamook, Neovia/Octave) are self-reported and unaudited; I rated them Low deliberately. The LTL damage rate of 1.24% and the 70-90% 'not our fault' figure both come from companies selling into this problem. The 3.5% receiving error rate is a model input in a peer-reviewed paper, not a measured field rate. Hardware prices were read in late 2026 and move quickly; the Coral price in particular was not shown on the vendor page I opened and came from a reseller listing. Every legal point marked confirmed:false is a place where I could not find a primary rule and the design should assume the conservative reading. This is research, not legal advice - camera placement, notice language and retention policy should be reviewed by a NJ employment lawyer before the first install.
data_gaps: Could not retrieve the Census County Business Patterns count of NAICS 493110 establishments specifically in Middlesex County - the Census API requires a key and returned 'Missing Key'. A third-party page citing Census CBP 2022 reports 1,548 establishments and 46,639 employees for the broader 48-49 sector, which is not the same measure.
No public pricing for Kargo, Arvist, Zimark, or CargoLens; the CargoLens page showed a per-site/unlimited-user model but not the dollar figure.
Could not open OSHA's establishment inspection search (HTTP 403), so the OSHA-record prospecting signal is unverified.

No peer-reviewed study of a deployed dock-door VLM system at a small 3PL was found; the strongest peer-reviewed numbers are lab/benchmark results (packaging structure 85%, damaged parcel mAP 93.7%, PatchCore 99.1% AUROC on MVTec AD) which do not transfer directly to a dusty dock.
No New Jersey case law or statute found on the evidentiary weight of AI-generated count/photo records in a freight claim or an employee discipline dispute.
Could not confirm whether NJ biometric surveillance bill S3182 (2024-2025 session) was enacted.
Did not verify the SciELO paper's publication year or its 1%-10% receiving error figures beyond the abstract page.
Install labor, PoE switch, cabling and UPS costs have no primary source in this file; they are carried as allowances inside the pilot cost range.
